In primary prevention, aspirin has acquired a Class IB recommendation in patients with evidence of coronary artery disease, but without a history of myocardial infarction or revascularization. Furthermore, clopidogrel has been indicated, for the first time, as a valid alternative to aspirin in patients who are intolerant or have possible side effects (Class IA). 4 In secondary prevention, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and clopidogrel remains the standard for post-percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) patients for at least 6 months. However, in patients at high bleeding risk and low ischaemic risk, a reduction of DAPT to 1–3 months is recommended, followed by monotherapy with a single antiplatelet (Class IA). Recent studies support this strategy, demonstrating that personalized treatment can reduce bleeding risk without reducing the benefit in terms of future cardiovascular events. 11

In parallel, drugs such as colchicine and semaglutide have acquired an increasingly important role. Colchicine, at a daily dose of 0.5 mg, has been shown to reduce major cardiovascular events in patients with stable atherosclerotic disease, 12 earning a Class IIa recommendation (level of evidence A). Semaglutide, on the other hand, is effective in reducing cardiovascular events 13 in non-diabetic, obese, or overweight patients, earning a Class IIa recommendation (level of evidence B).

Indications for myocardial revascularization Myocardial revascularization has a proven crucial role in the management of CCS. The new guidelines renew the prognostic indications, recommending invasive treatment for patients with ejection fraction (EF) > 35%, in the presence of high-risk coronary artery disease and/or evidence of extensive myocardial ischaemia (>10% left ventricular ischaemia).

In particular, revascularization is indicated in the following cases: significant stenosis (≥50%) of the left main (Class IA) multi-vessel disease with stenosis ≥70% (Class IA) single- or two-vessel disease involving the proximal segment of the anterior descending artery (Class IB). In these circumstances, revascularization has been shown to reduce the risk of spontaneous infarction and cardiovascular mortality, with a consequent improvement in long-term prognosis. 14 In patients with reduced EF (<35%), however, the available data are less robust. The therapeutic decision should therefore be made by a multidisciplinary team, considering the patient's comorbidities and individual preferences (Class IC).

With regard to the type of revascularization to be used, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is generally preferred, especially in diabetic patients, with high anatomical complexity, reduced EF, and low surgical risk. In cases of left main stenosis with complex coronary anatomy (SYNTAX > 22), CABG is the recommended therapeutic choice, while PCI is considered equivalent in cases with less complex anatomy (SYNTAX < 22, Class IA).

Although the ORBITA II study 15 has shown that myocardial revascularization can be effective even in symptomatic patients not treated with antianginal drugs, the guidelines suggest favouring revascularization only when pharmacological therapy is ineffective (Class IA). A further innovation introduced by the guidelines is the adoption of intracoronary imaging techniques, such as intravascular ultrasonography and optical coherence tomography, which allow guiding PCI in highly complex situations, such as the treatment of the left main, coronary bifurcations, or long lesions. 4

The patient with ANOCA/INOCA as mentioned in the previous paragraphs, the new CCS 2024 guidelines place greater attention, both in the diagnostic and therapeutic phase, on the subgroup of patients who do not present obstructive epicardial disease. In particular, they introduce the concept of INOCA/ANOCA by focusing on the patient's symptoms rather than on the sole evidence of ischaemia. For the first time, in patients with non-obstructive coronary artery disease who are persistently symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy, a complete invasive functional study is recommended to characterize the pathophysiological mechanism and define the endotype (Recommendation 1B). Reduced coronary reserve (coronary flow reserve < 2.5, with thermodilution or Doppler methods) can be caused by (i) reduced metabolic dilation of the microcirculation in response to increased myocardial oxygen consumption {in this case microvascular resistance during adenosine testing is elevated [index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR) > 25 with thermodilution or hyperemic microvascular resistance (hMR) > 2.5 with Doppler]}; (ii) high myocardial flow at rest probably caused by reduced metabolic oxygen utilization (in this case, IMR and hMR are normal). In addition to the two aforementioned endotypes, INOCA/ANOCA can be caused by two other endotypes: epicardial spasm or microvascular spasm, the diagnosis of which is based on the acetylcholine test ( Figure 3 ).
Figure 3 Diagnostic–therapeutic algorithm in ANOCA/INOCA patients (angina/ischaemia in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease).

The figure shows a diagnostic and therapeutic pathway for patients with suspected chronic ischaemic heart disease (chronic coronary syndrome) and persistent symptoms, structured in several phases. Phase 1. It is characterized by an initial clinical evaluation that includes the clinical history and risk factors, the exclusion of non-cardiac causes of the symptoms, the execution of the objective examination, and ECG. If the results suggest chronic coronary syndrome, further investigations are carried out. Phase 2. Execution of sequential tests (in any order): functional imaging: PET, magnetic resonance imaging, stress echo, and SPECT; anatomical imaging: coronary CT angiogram. Possible outcomes at the end of this step are diagnosis of coronary microvascular dysfunction and/or myocardial ischaemia with no or minimal obstructive coronary artery disease → ANOCA/INOCA; obstructive coronary artery disease → management with optimal medical therapy ± invasive coronary angiography. Phase 3. If the diagnosis confirms ANOCA/INOCA, treatment is continued to control symptoms and improve quality of life. If symptoms persist despite therapy, invasive functional tests are recommended to assess further coronary dysfunction. Phase 4. Performing functional tests: this section describes the use of invasive tests to identify the causes of coronary dysfunction, divided into abnormal vasodilation or abnormal vasoconstriction: abnormal vasodilation (decreased response to vasodilation): (1) endothelium-independent (with adenosine): coronary flow reserve < 2.5, index of microcirculatory resistance > 25, HMR > 2.5 and (2) endothelium-dependent (low-dose acetylcholine 2–20 μg intracoronary) and abnormal vasoconstriction (high-dose acetylcholine 100–200 μg) (1) epicardial: epicardial spasm and (2) microvascular: microcirculatory spasm. Conclusions In conclusion, the ESC 2024 guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of CCS offer a holistic and personalized approach in the management of patients with CCS, revisiting the risk stratification of probability of coronary artery disease, underlining the importance of a complete angiographic study and a personalized medicine approach aimed at setting up a specific pharmacological therapy for the precise pathophysiological mechanism of the disease.
